description: A game about exploring the solar system.
summary:
Space Explorer is a 3D game that takes you on a rocket trip through the solar system. From the cockpit you visit 13 stops: the Sun, the eight planets, three moons and the asteroid belt, and you can land on seven of them. At each stop you read short facts, all checked against NASA, and at the end you take a 10-question quiz and put your score on a class scoreboard. Classmates can play on their own tablets.

The game also has a Space Guide, an AI helper you can ask any question about space. Its AI runs on the laptop itself, not on the internet, and at start-up it picks the model that is fast enough for that computer. A safety helper keeps it on space topics and blocks unkind words, and nothing anyone asks is saved.

We built it with AI helpers that wrote and checked the code, while we decided what to build and tested every version. 975 automatic tests check that it all still works.
details:
What does it do or how does it work? Space Explorer is a game where you fly a rocket through the solar system. You sit in the cockpit and visit 13 stops: the Sun, all 8 planets, 3 moons and the asteroid belt. You can even land on 7 of them, like Mars and Titan. At every stop you read cool facts. At the end there is a quiz with 10 questions, and your score goes on the class scoreboard.

My favorite part is the Space Guide. It's an AI helper inside the game, and you can ask it anything about space, like "Why is Mars red?" It answers in three short sentences. The AI lives on the laptop, so it doesn't need the internet.

What benefits does it have?

  • You learn about space by exploring it, which is more fun than just reading.
  • If you're curious about something, you can ask the Space Guide right away.
  • It's safe for kids. The guide only talks about space, it stops unkind words, and it never saves what you ask.
  • It's free, and you don't need an account or the internet for the AI.
  • It runs on a normal laptop from one folder, so you don't have to install anything.

What is the intended impact of the project? I want other kids to think space is as exciting as I do. I also want to show that kids can use AI in a safe way, with a grown-up checking it.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Coding languages:
    • JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the game
    • C# for the Space Guide
    • Node.js runs the game.
    • Three.js makes the 3D planets.
    • .NET runs the Space Guide.
    • The AI brains are two small models called Phi-3.5-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B.
  • AI helpers: my dad and I used an AI coding helper called Claude to write the code, and another AI helper checked it, like a teacher marking homework. I was the boss: I said what the game should do, I played every version, and I said what to change, like the way the spaceship fly through the asteroids belt.
  • Testing: 975 tiny test programs check that everything still works.
  • Hardware: a Windows laptop and a tablet.

How is your project creative?

  • You don't just read about planets: you fly there and land on them.
  • The guide picks its own brain. When it starts, it tries a bigger brain and a smaller one and keeps the one that is fast enough for that computer. That way it works on any computer, even a slow one.
  • The fact book. Small AI brains sometimes get numbers wrong, so we gave it a fact book with real facts from NASA to read before it answers.
  • No internet needed. You can carry the whole game on a USB stick and play it on another computer without installing anything.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Safety: kids will use it, so the guide only talks about space, stops rude words and never saves questions. My dad tests it with a checklist before anyone uses it, because AI can still make mistakes.
  • Facts: we checked every fact on NASA's website.
  • Speed: answers have to come quickly, even on a slow computer, and the whole class can ask questions at the same time.
  • Easy to use: big buttons for tablets and short sentences that are easy to read.
  • If something goes wrong: the game still works if the AI or the Wi-Fi isn't working.
